summary:
Lunar Timewalker is a browser app that puts you on the Moon at moments of space history and shows why they happened. Stand beside Eagle as Apollo 11 touches down on 20 July 1969, watch
SN 1006 blaze in the lunar sky, follow the May 2024 solar storm, and simulate explosions in an Explosion Lab where the blast waves sweep past the planets. Teachers can replay each event
in class and explain it with real numbers.

For the Lunar Landing Site Navigator challenge, the same engine shows where and when a lander gets sunlight and contact with Earth. It compares up to six sites, or one site on several
dates: Sun and Earth elevation against the real skyline from NASA LRO LOLA data, solar power, the direct radio link, time to sunset and Earthset, and the share of sunlight and longest
loss of contact over the next lunar day. One click lands you on the 3D terrain at that place and moment. Positions are tested against JPL Horizons DE441.

It matters because planners need fast, trustworthy answers when a launch slips, and students learn best by standing where history happened: on open NASA data, in seven languages, in any
browser.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Lunar Timewalker is a browser app that turns space history into places you can stand in. Three parts share one engine and one set of NASA data:

• Stand inside history. Twelve events can be replayed: Apollo 11's descent, touchdown and lift-off (July 1969), the supernovae of 1006 and 1054, the Great Comet of 44 BC, Jupiter and Saturn meeting in 7 BC, five planets beside the Sun in May 2000, Mars at its closest in 2003, the 2018 Martian dust storm, the May 2024 solar storm, the 12 August 2026 solar eclipse seen from the Moon, sunrise at the lunar south pole, and Ingenuity's first flight on Mars. Each is staged before, during and after, with the Sun, Earth, planets and stars where they really were; on the Moon and Mars you walk on real terrain while it happens.

• Simulate explosions. The Explosion Lab sets off a Type Ia or Type II supernova, a gamma-ray burst or a solar eruption at a chosen distance, from inside the Solar System out to Betelgeuse and the Crab Nebula. A Sun-centred map shows the light front and the blast waves sweeping past the planets, with a timed list of what happens to each body and a "Predict: 5 questions" quiz for class. It is a model and says so; the flash is dimmed so the waves stay visible.

• Answer the challenge. The Lunar Landing Site Navigator compares up to six landing sites (Apollo, CLPS and other commercial landers, other countries' landings, south-pole targets or any typed coordinate), or one site on four dates. For each it shows the Sun's and Earth's elevation against the real skyline, the visible share of the Sun's disc, the power on a 1 m² panel, the direct radio link to Earth and the time to the next sunset and Earthset; over the next lunar day (29.5 days) it gives the sunlight share, the longest night, the Earth-visible share and the longest loss of contact, with a timeline strip. "Go there" lands you on the 3D terrain at that place and moment, where the telemetry shows the same numbers live as you walk.

HOW IT WORKS

• Terrain: NASA LRO LOLA global elevation (16 px/deg), LOLA 5 m/px polar models from NASA GSFC PGDA at Shackleton rim and the Shackleton–de Gerlache ridge, LROC colour; Mars on MGS MOLA elevation.

• Sky: the Sun, Moon, planets and Earth from astronomy-engine with the Moon's real orientation (libration included), checked in automated tests against JPL Horizons DE441; stars from NASA SVS Deep Star Maps 2020 (ESA Gaia) and the HEASARC Bright Star Catalogue; CME timings from NASA DONKI.

• Skyline: from any site the app marches outward along great circles to 100 km over the LOLA map, including the Moon's curvature (no air, so no refraction). A body counts as visible when more than 5 % of its disc clears the skyline; panel power is the solar constant at the Sun's distance × 30 % efficiency × the visible share of the disc.

• Every number is labelled MEASURED, COMPUTED or MODEL on screen, and the Sources dialog lists every dataset with its link.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

• Teachers get ready lessons: put the class on the Moon at 20:17 UT on 20 July 1969 and ask why the Sun was only 10.7° high (long shadows let the crew see the rocks), or set off a supernova at different distances and let students predict the outcome before they watch it. Spectator mode plays events hands-free on a classroom screen.

• Students see causes, not just pictures: why the south pole is hard (the Sun circles the horizon, and a ridge 0.3° high turns 397 W of solar power into 0 W within six hours), why Earth drops below the skyline, how far away a supernova must be to be harmless.

• Mission planners and the public get a fast, trustworthy first look at a site and date without learning several expert tools.

TOOLS, LANGUAGES AND HARDWARE

TypeScript, React, three.js (WebGL2, GLSL shaders), zustand, astronomy-engine, Vite and Vitest; Python (rasterio, NumPy, Pillow, tifffile, OpenCV, Astropy, SciPy) to prepare the NASA data once; GitHub Pages for hosting. No special hardware: it runs in a current desktop or laptop browser, and because the data ship with the app as static files, a school can also run it from a local copy.

HOW IT IS CREATIVE

• Space history becomes a place: you do not watch a clip of Apollo 11, you stand on the plain while Eagle comes down, under the real Sun and Earth of that minute.

• Playful and practical questions get answers from the same physics: "what if a star exploded nearby?" and "where should Artemis land?" use one ephemeris, one terrain and one honest labelling system.

• Game-like interaction (walking, a telescope, time-lapse, a time bar from 3000 BC to AD 2035) carries real data.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

• Scientific honesty: models are labelled as models, nothing is invented, and positions are tested against JPL Horizons.

• Accessibility and safety: seven languages (English, Turkish, German, French, Spanish, Italian, Russian), keyboard and touch controls, a "Reduce flashes" setting, and a dimmed explosion flash for photosensitive viewers and HDR screens.

• Classroom reality: no install, a tutorial, spectator mode.

• Open data and credit: every NASA and partner source is credited in the app with its link; the NASA insignia and JPL logos were painted out of the NASA 3D models.

• SI use: SI coding assistants helped write the code and the translations, and the demo narration is an AI voice; this is disclosed in the app, the README and the video.

Demo video and 7-slide deck: https://lunar-devo.github.io/demo/ · Source code (MIT licence): https://github.com/lunar-devo/lunar-timewalker
